Long read sequencing (PacBio)

Maxi-prepped plasmids containing the replicate barcoded libraries were digested using SalI

to linearize the plasmid prior to long-read sequencing. The linearized plasmids were prepped for

sequencing by the Bauer Core using a SMRTbell v3.0 kit. The resulting libraries were sequenced

using a PacBio Sequel IIe (Bauer Core). We used computational methods from previous reports

of SARS-CoV-2 deep mutational scanning experiments51,52 to link barcode regions with individual

variants.

Virus library generation

Previous work has shown that reducing the bottleneck of an eight-plasmid reverse genetics

system can increase the library generation efficiency47,53. To this end, we generated a 6-in-1 ~18.1

kb plasmid containing bidirectional cassettes of mouse-adapted A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8) PB2,

PB1, PB1, PA, NP, M, NS (pDM_RG070, plasmid maps can be found at

https://github.com/dpmaurer/imprinted_ab_escape). To generate this plasmid, we first removed

the PaqCI site from pHW195 (PR8 NP, a gift from Jesse Bloom) by site-directed mutagenesis

(Agilent). Then, we amplified the bidirectional cassettes with Q5 (NEB, #M0491L) and the

pHW2000 plasmid backbone such that the whole plasmid could be assembled in a one-pot golden

gate reaction with PaqCI (NEB, #R0745S). Due to repeated regions, we found it necessary to

propagate this plasmid in NEB Stable E. coli (NEB, #C3040H) at 30 °C in LB medium, using non-

baffled flasks. Maxi preps of this plasmid were always sequence confirmed by whole plasmid

sequencing (Primordium Labs).

To avoid jackpotting or bottlenecking effects, we transfected each replicate of each library

in 96-144 transfections in 6-well plates. A mixture of 600,000 HEK293T and 100,000 hCK cells


<!-- Page 115 -->


101

per well were seeded in poly-D-lysine coated 6-well plates (Greiner, #657940). The next day when

cells were ~60-80% confluent, each well was transfected dropwise with the following after a 15

minute room temperature incubation: 200 µl Opti-MEM containing 500 ng HA library plasmid,

500 ng NA plasmid for the particular strain, 3 µg pDM_RG070 (6-in-1 PR8 plasmid), 500 ng

hTMPRSS2 plasmid54, and 9 µl of TransIT-LT1 (MirusBio, #2306, 2:1 ratio). Transfections were

performed in batches so that transfection mixtures were not sitting too long. After ~16-18 hours,

the FBS-containing media was removed, the cells were washed with PBS, and flu media containing

1 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin was added. Approximately 48 hours after replacing the media when

cytopathic effect was apparent, the supernatants were pooled, clarified by centrifugation (800 xg,

5 min), aliquoted, and frozen at -80 °C to bank the “P0” stocks.

To enhance genotype-phenotype linkage, we passaged virus at a low MOI (0.01) across

approximately 200-300 million cells. To do this, we seeded 4000 cm2, 16-layered flasks (Greiner,

#678116) with ~50,000 hCK cells per cm2 in flu media. The next day, we infected these cells with

3 million infectious particles in 500 mls of flu media. After 1 hour, we removed the inoculum,

washed the cells with PBS, and replaced the media with fresh flu media containing 1 µg/ml TPCK-

trypsin. ~20-24 hours post-infection, we clarified the supernatant and aliquoted “P1” viral stocks.

These P1 stocks were used for escape selections we describe here.

Titering and neutralization assays

To titer or test neutralization against viral libraries, we used a standard ELISA-based

microneutralization assay55 with some modifications. hCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates

(Corning, #3595) at 20,000-30,000 cells per well in flu media. The next day, virus was prepared

in half-log dilutions (for titering) or at 200 TCID50 / 50 µl (neutralization) in flu media containing


<!-- Page 116 -->


102

2 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin. For viral neutralization assays, we used the viral libraries from replicate 1

of each background strain to test neutralization so that neutralization potencies are calculated with

the same material used for selections. Each neutralization assay was performed in quadruplicate.

Flu media (titering) or four-fold antibody dilutions (neutralization) were added to the viruses (1:1

ratio) and incubated at 37 °C / 5% CO2 for 1 hour. The media was then removed from the cells and

virus (tittering) or virus-antibody mixtures (neutralization) were overlayed on the hCK cells. After

1 hour at 37 °C / 5% CO2, the inoculum was removed, the cells were washed with PBS, and fresh

flu media containing 1 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin was added. ~18-20 hours later, the media was

removed, cells were washed twice with PBS, and fixed with ice-cold 80% acetone in PBS for 10

minutes. After removing the fixative and air-drying, the plates were washed with wash buffer (PBS

+ 0.3% Tween20 (Sigma, #P1379)) three times before adding antibody diluent (PBS + 0.1%

Tween20 + 1% BSA) to block. After blocking for 1 hour at room temperature, the plates were

washed three times and a solution of anti-nucleoprotein antibodies (Sigma, #MAB8257 and

#MAB8258, 1:4000 each) in antibody diluent were added for 1 hour at room temperature. After

washing three times, a dilution of anti-mouse antibody HRP conjugate (seracare, #5220-0339,

1:20000) was added for 1 hour at room temperature. After washing five times, Ultra TMB was

added (ThermoFisher, #34028) for ~15 minutes). The development was stopped by addition of 2M

sulfuric acid before reading at 450 nm (SpectraMax).

Titering calculations were performed by the Reed and Muench method55,56. Each dilution

was performed in quadruplicate or eight replicates. Neutralization potencies were determined by

subtracting background from cell only controls and normalizing 0% neutralization to the virus only

controls. IC50 values were determined by a sigmoidal curve fit in GraphPad Prism. IC99 values

were then determined by IC99 = (99/(100-99))(1/hill slope) x IC50.

Virus library selections

Escape selections were performed in T150 flasks after seeding 50,000 hCK cells per cm2

(~7.5 million) the day prior. A number of infectious particles corresponding to an MOI of ~0.05

were combined with antibody at 10x the IC99 value in a total of 28 mls of flu media containing

trypsin. After incubation (37 °C / 5% CO2) for 1 hour, the hCK cells were washed with PBS, and

new flu media containing trypsin was added. After ~20-24 hours, supernatant was clarified by

centrifugation and 20 mls were concentrated using 100K MWCO protein concentrators

(ThermoFisher, #88532) by centrifugation (1000 xg, 4 °C, 30-60 min). The viral RNA from the

supernatant was purified using QIAamp virla RNA mini preps (Qiagen, #52904). The final elution

was 60 µl using the supplied buffer.

Amplification of viral barcodes

To amplify the viral barcoded regions, potential DNA contamination was first removed by

incubation of 8 µl viral RNA, 1 µl ezDNase, and 1 µl ezDNase buffer (ThermoFisher, #11766051)

at 37 °C for 2 minutes. dNTPs (NEB, #N0447L, 1 µl), water (1 µl), and a primer that anneals in

the 3’ noncoding region (prDM370, 2 µM, 1 µl, Table S2) were added and incubated at 65 °C for

5 minutes before placing on ice for 1 minute. SuperScript IV (ThermoFisher, #18090050, 1 µl),

SuperScript IV buffer (4 µl), RNaseOUT (ThermoFisher, #10777019, 1 µl) and DTT (100 mM, 1

µl) were added to start cDNA synthesis by incubation at 50 °C for 30 minutes followed by 80 °C

for 10 minutes. The cDNA was cleaned up by a 1.6X AMPure XP bead cleanup (Beckman,

#A63881) with a final elution of 23 µl, of which 20 µl was recovered for the first PCR step.

To (1) increase the accuracy of amplicon sample assignment from NGS data, (2) increase

the nucleotide diversity during sequencing, and (3) limit amplification bias, we amplified the


<!-- Page 118 -->


104

barcoded region in a first PCR step with primers (Table S2) containing inline indices and cycled

only four times31. This first PCR step was performed using a standard Q5 () PCR: cDNA template

(20 µl), Q5 buffer (10 µl), dNTPs (10 mM, 1 µl), water (13.5 µl), primers (10 mM, 2.5 µl each),

and Q5 polymerase (0.5 µl) was combined. The reaction was cycled by 98 °C for 10 seconds; four

cycles of 98 °C for 30s, 67 °C for 10s, 72 °C for 10s; 72 °C for 2 minutes. The reaction was purified

with a 1.6X AMPure XP bead cleanup with a final elution of 23 µl, of which 20 µl was used for

the second PCR step. To calculate functional scores29, we also amplified the barcoded region from

the plasmid libraries using 10 ng as input for the first PCR step.

The second PCR step added NEBNext unique dual index primers onto the ends of the

amplicon (NEB, #E6440S). This was achieved by a two-step PCR reaction containing the same

reagents as in the first PCR step except the primers were 5 µl of the supplied unique dual index

primer mix. The cycling conditions were the following: 98 °C for 30s; 14 cycles of 98 °C for 10s,

72 °C for 15s; 72 °C for 2 minutes. We found that increasing cycles above 14 often resulted in the

formation of “bubble” products due to over amplification of the amplicon. The approximate

concentrations were determined by D1000 Tape on a TapeStation (Agilent). The amplicons were

pooled at equimolar concentrations and quantified using Qubit (ThermoFisher) prior to submission

for Illumina sequencing using a NovaSeq SP flow cell (Bauer Core).

We complexed UCA860 with MA90 at a Fab:HA head ratio of 4:1 and CH67 with MA90-

G189E at a ratio of 2:1 at room temperature for 30 minutes. The complexes were concentrated to

~12 mg/ml prior to crystallization. We used the hanging drop method in 96-well plates (Greiner,

Computational methods

The computational methods used here are largely based on previous computational

analyses from deep mutational scanning experiments9,29,51. These methods detail barcode linking

with PacBio sequencing data51, functional score calculations29, and differential selection

calculations9. We also used packages alignparse59 and dms_variants

(https://jbloomlab.github.io/dms_variants/). Jupyter notebooks and outputs for the code described

below are available at https://github.com/dpmaurer/imprinted_ab_escape.

Linking barcodes to variants

The PacBio data generated as above was used to link the barcodes with respective variants.

We used alignparse59 version 0.6.2, based on previously written code from Starr et al.51,  to link

the barcoded region to individual variants. We removed variants with insertions but not deletions

as we intended to include deletions in our libraries. For each library, >10X coverage of the codon

variant library size had at least 3 PacBio CCSs per barcode.

Barcode count analysis

We merged paired end reads using PEAR60. From merged reads, we filtered for the

expected length based on the amplicon, inline indices, and UMIs. We additionally filtered out

sequences containing ambiguous base calls or those that did not match the expected inline indices.


<!-- Page 121 -->


107

From these filtered reads, we combined UMIs from each side of the amplicon into a single UMI

and counted unique barcode-UMI reads.

Functional score calculation

We determined functional scores using dms_variants

(https://jbloomlab.github.io/dms_variants/), which calculates the base 2 log enrichment before and

after selection compared to wild-type. In our case, pre-selection was the plasmid library and post-

selection was after generation and a low MOI passage. We calculated functional score by amino

acid substitutions and calculated synonymous variants separate from wild-type.

Differential selection calculation

We determined escape by using the metric of differential selection9

(https://jbloomlab.github.io/dms_tools2/diffsel.html). This metric calculates the enrichment of

each amino acid variant compared to wild-type between a selection and a “mock” selection (here,

a passage without added antibody). A pseudocount (we used a pseudocount of 10) is added to each

variant count that is scaled by read depth for a certain position. For analyses, we only considered

those variants that were positively selected (differential selection > 0) in both biological replicates

and all other values were set to 0. For each selection, we normalized the maximum differential

selection value to 1. We defined escape mutations as those that were >0.5 in both replicates. After

normalization, we summed the differential selection values at each site.

## ABSTRACT

Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting hemagglutinin (HA) of influenza viruses have the

potential to be used as therapies or templates for next-generation vaccines aimed at providing broad

protection. H1 and H3 influenza A viruses (IAVs) are subtypes currently circulating within the

human population and the focus of current seasonal vaccines. Here, we isolate pan-subtype mAbs

from human B cells targeting the H1 and H3 head domains as well as a mAb targeting the stem

that neutralizes group 2 IAVs. Pan-H1 mAbs target the lateral patch and recognize H1 HAs from

1933 to 2021 including an H1 HA from a swine IAV with pandemic potential. Using directed

evolution we improved the neutralization potency of the pan-H1 mAbs towards a contemporary

strain. We additionally used deep mutational scanning of four H1N1 viruses for both epitope

mapping and to identify positions that could potentially escape this class of mAb. We used cryo-

EM to determine the pan-H3 mAb epitopes and show that one targets the side of the H3 head,

accommodating the N133 glycan and pocket underneath the 130 loop of the receptor binding site.

The group 2 neutralizing mAb targets an epitope that overlaps with previously characterized

mAbs, but with distinct antibody variable genes and mode of recognition, inserting its CDRH3

into a groove at the base of HA. These mAbs identify common sites recognized by pan-subtype

mAbs that may be elicited by next-generation vaccines.

## INTRODUCTION

The low effectiveness of seasonal influenza vaccination, amongst other factors, leads to

approximately half of a million deaths caused by influenza viruses worldwide each year1. Of the

two influenza types that cause human disease, influenza A viruses (IAVs) are responsible for

pandemics emerging from animal reservoirs in contrast to influenza B viruses (IBVs) that only

circulate in humans. Antigenic and genetic differences of the major surface glycoprotein,

hemagglutinin (HA), which engages the sialic acid receptor and fuses the viral and endosomal

membranes, further divide IAVs into two distinct groups with 18 HA subtypes (H1-H18) total. In

the last century, IAVs bearing H1 or H2 (group 1), or H3 (group 2) HAs have circulated in the

human population, with H1N1 and H3N2 viruses currently circulating.

Vaccine effectiveness against seasonal influenza viruses only reaches modest levels around

50%2. Repeated updating of annual vaccines is primarily due to antigenic drift – the acquisition of

amino acid mutations in HA that preserve function but escape population-wide antibody

recognition. IAVs undergo antigenic drift more rapidly than IBVs3, requiring continuous

monitoring for new antigenic variants. Additional barriers to an effective vaccine include variable

immune histories and adaptation mutations during vaccine production. A complementary approach

to seasonal vaccination is to identify monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that target conserved HA sites

and used prophylactically or therapeutically. Characterizing such mAbs can also serve as templates

to guide next-generation vaccine designs and inform how viral escape from population immunity

may occur.

mAbs that target the HA “head” domain and prevent sialic acid receptor engagement, is an

established correlate of protection, but are often subtype specific4-6. mAbs with heterosubtypic

breadth often bind epitopes on the membrane proximal “stem” within group 1, group 2, or, in some


<!-- Page 132 -->


118

cases, all influenza HAs7-11, that can inhibit fusion in vitro but not receptor binding. Although these

mAbs are protective in mice7-11, they often require Fc-effector functions for protection, suggesting

that although stem-targeting mAbs can neutralize in vitro, there is minimal neutralization activity

in vivo12. Due to their reactivity to potentially pandemic IAVs that have not circulated in humans,

stem-directed mAbs may provide an added layer of protection from severe disease in the case of

zoonotic spillover or viral escape from anti-head mAbs. Consistently, head-directed mAbs from

humans better protect against acquiring infection when compared to stem-directed mAbs even

when normalized by binding titers, but passive transfer of stem-directed mAbs still maintained

some level of protection13.

In contrast to anti-stem mAbs, IAVs escape anti-head mAbs frequently in Nature,

demonstrating that these mAbs provide a significant barrier for transmission that the virus must

overcome to persist in the population3,14,15. Although epitopes in the head are less conserved than

the stem, it is still possible to identify pan-subtype anti-head mAbs, which covers all IAVs

currently circulating within the human population. Indeed, previous work has identified some

head-targeting mAbs against H116-22 and H323-25 HAs. Epitopes on the side of the HA head (e.g.,

the lateral patch, vestigial esterase) are conserved20,23,24, affording mAbs targeting these sites

considerable breadth; next-generation vaccine approaches elicit antibodies targeting these

conserved epitopes 26-28. However, if these vaccines were to be used on a large scale, it is unclear

how such a polyclonal response may recognize HA and how the virus would escape.

Here, we isolate and characterize pan-H1 and -H3 mAbs from human donors. For the pan-

H1 mAbs, which neutralize human H1N1 IAVs spanning ~100 years, we used four deep

mutational scanning H1N1 viral libraries to map critical residues within the targeted epitope.

Although escape from pan-H1 mAbs was readily selected, human isolates rarely had escape


<!-- Page 133 -->


119

mutations. Pan-H1 mAb neutralizing potency could be improved against a contemporary H1N1

strain using directed evolution. For the pan-H3 mAbs, which neutralize human H3N2 IAVs

spanning ~50 years, we determined cryo-EM structures in complex with HA. One pan-H3 mAb

targets an epitope in the head domain with regions of low mutational tolerance29. The other pan-

H3 mAb targets the group 2 stem site but engages with a distinct mode of recognition. We also

identify potential amino acid positions that may acquire escape mutations if immune pressure at

these sites increases. The epitopes identified by these pan-H3 mAbs overlap with those targeted

by previously characterized mAbs, but with different antibody variable gene usage and paratopes,

suggesting antibodies targeting these sites may have variable escape mutations, thus raising the

barrier to escape.

## RESULTS

Isolation of H1 and H3 monoclonal antibodies

To identify pan-subtype neutralizing mAbs, we used a panel of reporter IAVs spanning

1933 to 2021 that includes distinct antigenic clusters3, representing IAVs that have previously

escaped humoral immunity. We sorted H1-reactive B cells from human PBMCs using recombinant

full-length HAs derived from A/California/07/2009. We then sequenced the variable genes,

recombinantly produced mAbs30 and screened for neutralization activity. H1-targeting mAbs were

screened against representative H1N1 strains A/WSN/1933, A/Solomon Islands/3/2006, and

A/Michigan/45/2015. We identified two clonally related mAbs, ADI-77470 and ADI-77474, that

completely neutralized (>99%) all three H1N1 viruses at 1 µg/ml used for screening (Figure

3.1A).


<!-- Page 134 -->


120

To isolate pan-H3 mAbs, we sorted B cells using recombinant HA probes from H3N2s

A/Hong Kong/1/1968 (HK68) and A/Darwin/6/2021 (DAR21) coupled to different fluorophores

to specifically sort cross-reactive B cells. The HK68 probe included the HA head fused to a foldon

trimerization tag, allowing us to specifically sort head-directed mAbs in addition to those that

target full-length DAR21 HA. These efforts resulted in two pan-H3 mAbs, ADI-85647 and ADI-

85666, that were further characterized (Figures 3.1B and 3.1C).

We characterized the subtypic neutralization potency of these pan-H1 and -H3 mAbs,

against 11 H1N1 or 10 H3N2 IAVs. The pan-H1 mAbs potently neutralized all H1N1s, but not a

representative H3N2; the pan-H3 mAbs neutralized all H3N2 viruses tested, but not a

representative H1N1 (Figure 3.2A). To further test the breadth of these mAbs, we screened for

binding by ELISA to the H1 HA from an swine H1N1 with pandemic potential

(A/Swine/HN/SN13/201831) or an H3 HA from a canine H3N2 found to evolve mammalian-like

traits (A/Canine/Hainan/79/201932). Although these IAVs have never circulated in humans, these

mAbs bound these strains, highlighting their considerable breadth (Figure 3.2B). We performed

competition assays to crudely map the region on HA targeted by these mAbs. The pan-H1 mAbs

competed with 047-09M-2F0317, a mAb targeting the lateral patch of H1 HAs. ADI-85647

competed with F005-12633, H3v-4723, and C58524, which target the H3 head, whereas ADI-85666

competed with MEDI885210, demonstrating that it targets the stem (Figure 3.2C). ADI-85666

additionally neutralized a group 2 H7N9 IAV which is consistent with other stem-targeting mAbs

(Figure 3.2A).

Viral escape from pan-H1 antibodies

We next more finely mapped pan-H1 mAbs by viral escape. We previously

generated deep mutational scanning viral libraries of three H1N1s containing all single amino acid

mutations and deletions in the HA head (residues 52-263, H3 numbering): A/USSR/90/1977

(USSR77), A/Siena/10/1989 (SN89), and A/Solomon Islands/3/2006 (SI06). Here, we additionally

generated a viral library in the background of A/Sydney/5/2021 (SYD21) to determine whether

escape is different in a post-2009 pandemic H1N1 (Figure 3.3A). These strains represent four

distinct H1N1 antigenic clusters. We passaged these viral libraries in the presence of either ADI-

77470 or ADI-77474 at 10x the IC99 to identify escape variants (Figures 3.3 and 3.4). Mutation

of P122 to either acidic residues or deletion was the most selected in all virus backgrounds (Figure

3.4). However, ADI-77474 was more sensitive to mutational escape in SYD21 compared to its

clonal relative ADI-77470 (Figures 3.3 and 3.4). Furthermore, although escape primarily occurred

at position 122, mutation to Asn at 122, 123, and 124 in SYD21 escaped both mAbs; each of these

Asn mutations introduces a predicted N-linked glycosylation sequon. Although 123N and 124N

mutations in the historical strains USSR77, SN89, and SI06 also create predicted N-linked

glycosylation sites, these mutations were not enriched in these strains, demonstrating different

barriers to escape by glycosylation for pre- and post-pandemic H1s (Figure 3.4C).

We mapped the escape mutations onto a structure of a mAb targeting the same epitope and

uses the same germline V-genes17 (Figure 3.4B). Residues 119, 122-125, and 172 cluster around

the YxR motif often found in this class of mAbs17, although the mAbs we describe have a similarly

charged YxK motif in the CDRH3.

Affinity maturation of pan-H1 mAbs increases neutralization potency

To increase the affinity of pan-H1 mAbs, we generated yeast display libraries encoding

mutations in the variable heavy and light chain genes and selected variants with increased binding

affinity using recombinant SYD21 HA head34. We down-selected affinity-matured mAbs based

on a single replicate neutralization screen against SYD21 virus (Figure 3.5) and further tested

these mAbs against the historical H1N1 A/Beijing/262/1995 (Figure 3.6A). ADI-86325 had 2

light- and 4 heavy-chain mutations relative to ADI-77470, which increased the potency by ~4-fold

while maintaining BE95 neutralization (Figure 3.6A). We next assessed whether in vitro affinity

maturation of ADI-77470 to ADI-86325 affected viral escape due to its increased potency by using

the deep mutational scanning SYD21 library. We found that despite this increased potency, highly

selected escape mutations were nevertheless similar (Figure 3.6B).

To determine the frequency of escape mutations in IAV isolates, we queried  the GISAID

database for unique H1Nx sequences from human or swine isolates and calculated the frequency

of mutations at positions 119, 122-125, and 172 (Figure 3.6C). The escape mutation with the

highest frequency in humans, 125E, was identified at a frequency of ~0.18% of unique H1Nx

sequences, suggesting human immunity rarely selects for these mutations. Swine isolates had

frequencies reaching ~3% of unique sequences with 123N and 124N being the most highly

represented.

A pan-H3 mAb targets the side of the H3 HA head

As deep mutational scanning libraries for historical and contemporary H3N2 viruses were

unavailable, we used cryo-EM to structurally determine the epitopes targeted by the pan-H3 mAbs.

ADI-85647 in complex with DAR21 HA shows that it binds to the side of the HA head, consistent

with competition with H3v-47, C585, and F005-126 (Figures 3.7A). During antigenic drift of H3

HA, potential N-linked glycosylation sites were acquired and maintained in this site at positions

122, 126, and 133. Although the density map was well-defined for glycosylation at N133, we did

not observe glycan density at N122, consistent with a previous report showing no and full glycan

occupancy at N122 and N133, respectively35. The N133 glycan sits within a cleft between the

variable heavy and light chains, and the CDRH2 inserts between the N133 and N126 glycans

(Figure 3.7B). The Y32 hydroxyl and V2 backbone in the heavy chain form hydrogen bonds with

the GlcNAc and mannose, respectively, and thus stabilizing it within this cleft. There are eleven

hydrogen bonds, two of which are with the N133 glycan; no salt bridges are observed. The heavy

chain contributes only two hydrogen bonds and interacts with HA with several aromatic residues

(Figure 3.7C). W102 in the CDRH3 sits within a pocket underneath the 130-loop. While the ADI-

85647 epitope overlaps with H3v-4723, it can neutralize H3N2 strains prior to 1989 in contrast to

H3v-4723 (Figures 3.7D and 3.7E).While this conserved pocket also has low mutational tolerance

determined by a previous study29 we observe that mutations at positions 80, 122, 124, and 141

have higher mutational tolerance, suggesting that mAbs targeting this site may ultimately select

for escape at these positions (Figure 3.7F).

Group 2 neutralization through a unique structural solution

The anti-stem mAb ADI-85666 uses unique germline gene usages, VH4-61 and VK1-17,

not previously reported for group 2 anti-stem mAbs; we therefore determined a cryo-EM structure

to understand how recognition differs from previously reported mAbs (Figure 3.8A). The epitope

overlaps with recognition of other group 2 bnAbs11,38, such as CR8020, but the CDRH3 of ADI-

85666 extends into a groove spanning the β-sheet at the base of the stem located near the viral

membrane (Figures 3.8B and 3.8C). The Tyr at the tip of the CDRH3 makes a stabilizing sulfur-

aromatic contact with M133 (HA2 numbering) (Figure 3.8C). One side of the CDRH3 interacts

with the hydrophobic groove with I07 and F109 in the CDRH3 while the other side forms a Glu-

Arg-Tyr triad with Arg25 of HA. A second Glu-Arg-Tyr triad is formed with E15 of the fusion

peptide and residues Y34 and R99 in the CDRH2 and CDRH3, respectively (Figure 3.8C).

Comparison of the interfacing residues of ADI-85666 with CR8020 shows overlap of the

outermost β-sheet strand but diverge towards the central strands or G-helix for ADI-85666 or

CR8020, respectively (Figure 3.8D). This epitope is conserved in WHO recommended vaccine

strains of H3N2s (Figure 3.8E), but the residues surrounding the hydrophobic groove have a

higher mutational tolerance29 (Figure 3.8F). Specific mutations within this interface may escape

mutational tolerance, suggesting that a mutation that removes this salt bridge or that changes its

## DISCUSSION

Here, we isolate pan-H1 and -H3 neutralizing mAbs from human donors and characterize

the targeted epitopes by viral escape and cryo-EM. Pan-H1 mAbs potently neutralize all tested

H1N1 strains from 1933 to 2021 and bind to a pre-pandemic swine HA. Despite conservation of

the lateral patch recognized by pan-H1 mAbs, viral escape occurred readily, primarily at position

122. We increased the affinity of the pan-H1 mAbs, increasing neutralization potency to a

contemporary H1 HA. This affinity-matured mAb, ADI-86325, selected for viral escape mutations

P122D/E/-, 125D/E, and Asn mutations at 122-124, which introduce potential N-linked

glycosylations; these mutations have rarely been found in human IAV isolates. Structural

characterization of the pan-H3 anti-head mAb, ADI-85647, shows that engagement of a conserved

pocket underneath the 130-loop of the receptor binding site (RBS) is a target for broad H3 mAbs

binding this conserved site. The structure of the group 2 anti-stem mAb, ADI-85666, shows the

CDRH3 inserts into a groove not contacted by previously characterized group 2 anti-stem mAbs.

Comparing these epitopes with pre-existing deep mutational scanning data29 identifies sites likely

to escape these mAbs. Together with previously determined structures of broad H3 mAbs11,23,38,

our data show that mAbs recognize these conserved H3 HA sites in different manners, which could

allow a polyclonal antibody response to raise the barrier to escape.

The 2009 H1N1 pandemic recalled cross-reactive B cell responses that targeted the RBS

and lateral patch17,20,39. However, upon subsequent exposures, these responses became absent17,

which likely contributed to the conservation of the lateral patch epitope. Next-generation vaccines

using mosaic nanoparticles containing antigenically distinct H1 HA heads elicited B cells targeting

the lateral patch in animal models26,27. In humans, initial recall of lateral patch-directed mAbs after

the pandemic selected for viral escape through the addition of an N-linked glycosylation20.


<!-- Page 152 -->


138

However, a subset of lateral patch-directed mAbs, primarily encoded by VH3-23/VK1-33,

overcome this escape17. It is therefore possible that the use of these mosaic nanoparticle vaccine

candidates in humans may preferentially elicit VH3-23/VK1-33 responses. The two clonally related

mAbs encoded by VH3-23/VK1-33 genes we discovered here drove escape largely at the positions

engaged by the common YxR motif in this class of mAb (119, 122, 125, and 172), independent on

the background strain. Despite further affinity maturation, these mAbs were readily escaped in

contrast to affinity maturation of RBS-directed mAbs that we have previously shown can increase

the barrier to escape (Chapter 2). These data suggest that next-generation vaccines or therapeutic

mAbs targeting this site may not provide long-term broad protection. However, if population-wide

immune pressure on this site does not increase, lateral-patch mAbs may nevertheless serve as

potent therapeutics for high-risk populations. Future studies are needed to understand whether

there are mAbs that target this site and are insensitive to the escape mutations described here while

retaining their broad reactivity.

Comparison of the structures of ADI-85647 and H3v-47 show that both insert hydrophobic

residues into a conserved pocket underneath the 130 loop. ADI-85647, but not H3v-47, recognizes

strains prior to 198923, highlighting that these mAbs are sensitive to different mutations within this

epitope. As noted previously, the H3 head domain appears to be more mutationally intolerant than

the stem; this is in contrast to H1s29. This conservation and mutational intolerance within the

pocket targeted by these mAbs may be a result of the proximity to the conserved W153 in the

receptor binding pocket; Therefore, mAbs targeting this pocket with differing V-genes, angles of

approach, and mutation sensitivities may be an additional way to target H3N2s with escape

resistance, reminiscent of a polyclonal antibody response to the RBS pocket21. Notably, although

ADI-85647 targets a site on H3 similar to that targeted by H1 lateral patch-directed mAbs, the


<!-- Page 153 -->


139

neutralization potency is markedly lower. While in vitro affinity maturation of ADI-85647 may

increase potency it is possible that H1N1 and H3N2 viruses are differentially neutralized by mAbs

targeting these sites.

The group 2 mAb, ADI-85666, targets an epitope that overlaps with that of other group 2

neutralizing mAbs, CR802011 and CR804338, but has an extended CDRH3 that reaches into a

groove not contacted by other mAbs; this is the third structurally characterized group 2 mAb that

targets this site, each with distinct epitopes. The gene usage and diversity of recognition suggests

that a polyclonal antibody response to this site may be resistant to escape. We note, however, that

a recent clinical trial of a prophylactic pan-influenza stem-targeting bnAb, VIR2482 (a version of

MEDI885210) failed to significantly reduce IAV illness (NCT05567783). Therefore, although we

do not expect group 2 mAbs, or vaccines that elicit them, to prevent disease, they may afford an

important bridge during seasons of large antigenic change or in the case of spillover of a subtype

for which humans have limited immunity. Altogether, these pan-subtypic neutralizing mAbs could

be used in prophylactic and/or therapeutic applications. Furthermore, these mAbs, the viral escape

mutations, and structurally characterized epitopes can be used as tools for designing next-

generation vaccines.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

Cell lines and media

Cell lines HEK293T, HEK293T-PB1, MDCK-SIAT1-PB1, and MDCK-SIAT1-H7 (gifts from

Jesse Bloom and Masaru Kanekiyo) were maintained in DMEM (Gibco) with 10% heat-

inactivated FBS (Peak), and penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco). For the growth of MDCK-SIAT1-

PB1 and MDCK-SIAT1-H7 cells, 1 mg/ml geneticin (Gibco) and 0.25 µg/ml puromycin (Gibco)

were additionally added. For neutralization assays, “flu media” was used, which contains Opti-

MEM (Gibco), 0.3% BSA (Sigma), penicillin/streptomycin, 0.1 mg/ml CaCl22, and 0.01% heat-

inactivated FBS (Peak).

Generation of influenza reporter viruses

Influenza reporter viruses were generated similar to a previous report40. Briefly, reverse

genetics bidirectional pHW plasmids (gifts from Jesse Bloom and Masaru Kanekiyo) encoding the

HA and NA of each strain, the internal segments from A/WSN/1933, tdKatushka2 with PB1

packing sequences, and a plasmid that drives expression of human TMPRSS2 were transfected

into a co-culture of HEK293T-PB1 (a gift from Jesse Bloom) and MDCK-SIAT1-PB1 cells (a gift

from Masaru Kanekiyo) in 6-well plates using TransIT-LT1 (MirusBio) at a 2:1 ratio. For H1N1s,

the non-coding regions from A/WSN/1933 were used and for H3N2s, the non-coding regions from

A/Netherlands/009/2010 were used. The virus-containing supernatant was harvested after three

days, clarified by centrifugation, and added to a confluent monolayer of MDCK-SIAT1-PB1 cells

seeded the day prior. Once cytopathic effect was evident (two to three days), the supernatant was

clarified and stored at -80 °C. To safely generate an H7N9 virus in a BSL2 setting, we used the

pHW plasmid encoding tdKatushka with HA packing sequences, the A/Shanghai/02/103 NA, the


<!-- Page 155 -->


141

internal genes from mouse-adapted PR8, and propagated the virus using the MDCK-SIAT-H7 cell

line that expresses cell-surface H7 HA.

Virus titering and neutralization

Titering and neutrlaization assays were performed in a similar manner as previously

described40. 20,000-30,000 MDCK-SIAT1-PB1 cells were seeded in 96-well plates (CellVis) in

flu media. For virus titering, virus stocks were thawed the next day and diluted in a twofold series

in quadruplicate. Flu media containing 2 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin (Sigma) was then added to the virus

dilutions at a 1:1 ratio. After incubation at 37 °C / 5% CO2 for one hour, 100 µl of virus/media

was added. After ~18-20 hours, the cells were imaged on a CellDiscoverer7 (Zeiss) and fluorescent

tdKatushka positive cells were counted using Zeiss software. The cell counts were then plotted

and a sigmoidal curve was fit to the data to determine the amount of virus that generated half

maximal infection (GraphPad Prism). This dilution was used for subsequent neutralization assays.

Neutralization assays were performed similar to titering assays. Virus was mixed 1:1 with

corresponding mAb concentrations prior to the one hour incubation period. After counting cells as

described above, cell counts for negative control wells (no virus added) were subtracted from all

wells, and percent neutralization was counted by normalizing 0% neutralization to positive control

wells and 100% neutralization to negative control wells. These data were plotted and fit in

GraphPad Prism to determine the IC50 values.

Influenza virus library generation

The deep mutational scanning HA head library of A/Sydney/5/2021 was generated as

described in Chapter 2. Briefly, the HA coding sequence library (Twist Bioscience) was cloned by


<!-- Page 156 -->


142

a golden gate reaction (NEB) into a modified pHW2000 plasmid41 with non-coding regions

derived from PR8 and a barcoded region after the stop codon. E. coli (NEB 10-beta) were

electroporated (BioRad) twice, each with half of the golden gate reaction to generate replicate

libraries. E. coli carrying plasmid libraries were plated in large 245 mm agar plates (Corning) and

colonies were counted. Approximately 200,000 colonies for each replicate were scraped into LB

media and grown for an additional two hours before maxi prepping the plasmid libraries. Plasmid

libraries were digested with SalI and submitted to the Bauer Core for long-read PacBio sequencing

on a Sequel IIe.

The HA plasmid libraries, A/Sydney/5/2021 NA, the internal segments of mouse-adapted

PR8 in a single plasmid (see Chapter 2), and a plasmid expressing human TMPRSS240 were

transfected (TransIT-LT1, MirusBio, 2:1 ratio) >96 times into the wells of six well plates

containing a 6:1 mixture of HEK293T: humanized MDCK cells42 seeded the day prior. The next

day, media was removed and replaced with flu media supplemented with 1 µg/ml TPCK-trypsin

to enable multi-cycle viral growth. Two days later, the supernatants from each well were pooled

by replicate and frozen in aliquots (“P0” stock). The P0 stock was then titered and passaged at an

MOI of 0.01 in ~2-3 x 106 humanized MDCK cells over 4000 cm2 (Greiner). The next day, the

supernatant was collected, pooled, and mixed before aliquoting and storing at -80 °C (“P1” stock).

These P1 stocks were used for viral escape assays.

ELISA

High-binding plates (Corning) were coated with 2 µg/ml of full-length soluble ectodomain

for HAs (A/Swine/HN/SN13/201831 or A/Canine/Hainan/79/201932) overnight at 4 °C. The next

day, the HAs were removed and blocking buffer (1% BSA and 0.1% Tween20 in PBS) was added


<!-- Page 157 -->


143

and incubated for one hour at room temperature. Then, the blocking buffer was removed and mAbs

were added for one hour at room temperature. The mAbs were washed out three times with wash

buffer (0.1% Tween20 in PBS), before adding anti-human IgG HRP conjugate (Abcam) at a

1:20000 dilution and incubating for one hour at room temperature. Excess HRP conjugate was

washed out with wash buffer three times before adding room temperature one-step ABTS

(ThermoFisher). After development, the absorbance values were read on a SpectraMax plate

reader. Background absorbance values, measured from wells containing no primary antibody, were

subtracted from other wells.

Deep viral escape assay

The deep viral escape assay was performed as described in Chapter 2. In T150 flasks

containing a monolayer of humanized MDCK cells, we mixed infectious particles corresponding

to an MOI of 0.05 in flu media with 2 µg/ml trypsin with an equivalent volume of mAb at 2X the

IC99 in flu media, totaling 28 mls. The antibody was allowed to bind to the virions for 1 hour at 37

°C / 5% CO2 before washing cells with PBS and adding the antibody/virus mixture. After 1 hour

to allow for initial infection, the cells were washed with PBS and fresh flu media with 1 µg/ml

TPCK-trypsin was added. After 20 hours, the supernatant was collected and concentrated with

100K MWCO concentrators (ThermoFisher) before extracting viral RNA (Qiagen). The barcoded

region was amplified as described below.

Viral barcode amplification

Barcode amplification was performed as described in Chapter 2. Briefly, reverse

transcription was carried out using superscript IV (Thermofisher), priming at the 3’ noncoding


<!-- Page 158 -->


144

region of the influenza HA viral RNA. The cDNA was purified from the reaction using a 1.6X

AMPure XP bead cleanup (Beckman). We used Q5 (NEB) to initially amplify the barcoded region

and append unique molecular identifiers in four rounds of amplification. The first PCR product

was purified using 1.6X AMPure XP beads. In the second PCR step, we used NEBNext unique

dual index primers to amplify the barcoded region and append Illumina adapters. The resulting

product was cleaned with 1.6X AMPure XP beads, and quantified by D1000 Tape (Agilent) and

Qubit (ThermoFisher). The resulting products were pooled at equimolar ratios and submitted for

sequencing on a NovaSeq 6000 (Bauer Core).

Protein production

HA coding sequences were cloned into a pVRC8400 vector with C-terminal tags: his tag,

3C cleavage site, foldon. HA monomeric head proteins used for in vitro affinity maturation instead

had C-terminal tags: 3C cleavage site, his tag, AviTag. Proteins were produced by transient

transfection into HEK293F (ThermoFisher) using PEI (3:1 ratio) or Expi293F using expifectamine

according to the manufacturer’s recommendations (ThermoFisher). Secreted HA was purified

from the supernatant using TALON metal affinity resin (Takara) and further purified over an S200

column on an AKTA pure (Cytiva). The H3 A/Darwin/6/2021 HA used in cryo-EM studies was

produced with a C-terminal 3C cleavage site and his tag without a foldon tag, but carried trimer

stabilizing mutations H26W, K51I, and E103I43. For cryo-EM studies, tags were cleaved off using

HRV 3C protease (ThermoFisher) and purified again over TALON resin and an S200 column.


<!-- Page 159 -->


145

HA conservation and mutational tolerance analyses

To determine frequencies of escape mutations that have occurred in sequenced H1 HAs,

we downloaded all H1 sequences isolated from human and swine that were deposited into

GISAID37. We removed duplicate sequences and calculated the frequency of escape mutations in

the resulting list of unique HAs.

To determine conservation amongst H3 HAs, we assembled a list of all vaccine strain

recommendations by the WHO (https://www.who.int/teams/global-influenza-

programme/vaccines/who-recommendations). We downloaded all available HA sequences in

GISAID from this list. The sequences were then aligned in Geneious and the percent identity

calculated. We then mapped the percent identity values onto the structure of H3 DAR21 in

PyMOL.

To determine mutational tolerances, we downloaded the amino acid preferences

determined by deep mutational scanning in H3N2 A/Perth/16/200929 available at

https://github.com/jbloomlab/Perth2009-DMS-Manuscript and calculated the Shannon Entropy at

each position as described29. We mapped the entropies (mutational tolerances) onto the structure

of H3 DAR21 in PyMOL and colored with a minimum of ≤1.05 and a maximum of ≥1.25.

CryoEM sample preparation and data collection

The recombinant HA (rHA) full length soluble ectodomain (FLsE) of H3/Darwin/6/2021 was

incubated with ADI-85647 or ADI-85666 Fab at a molar ratio 1:1.5 and a final protein

concentration of 2.5mg/ml for 30 minutes on ice. Immediately before depositing the sample onto

UltrAUFoil R1.2/1.3, 400 mesh gold grids coated with 2nm continuous carbon, octyl-beta-

glucoside was added to the pre-formed complex at 0.083% (w/v) final concentration. Three


<!-- Page 160 -->


146

microliters of the sample were applied on the gold face of the grids, blotted for 6 seconds on the

same face of the grid, at 20˚ C and 100% humidity, then plunge-frozen in 100% liquid ethane using

a Vitrobot Mark IV plunge freezer. The grids were first screened on an Artica Talos microscope

equipped with a Gatan K3 camera and operated at 200 kV. The highest quality grid was then

imaged using a Titan Krios microscope operated at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 Summit

direct electron detector. A total of 7,772 and 4,435 movies for the ADI-85647 or ADI-85666

complex, respectively, were collected in counting mode at 30 e-/px/s for a total dose of 52.44

e−/Å2/s. Images were collected at a magnification of 81000, corresponding to a calibrated pixel

size of 0.825 Å/pixel. Defocus values ranged between -1 and -2.5 µm.

CryoEM data processing

The data were processed using cryoSPARC v4.3.144. Briefly, the movies were aligned and

corrected for both global and local motion using Patch Motion Correction within cryoSPARC.

Then, contrast transfer function estimation was done using Patch CTF and particles were picked

using blob picker. The picked particles were extracted with a box size 400 pixels and 4x binned

for 2D classification. Two rounds of 2D classification were performed and the good particles were

selected for the generation of the initial model at 12 Å/pixel with 3 classes. Non-uniform

refinement was performed in C1 symmetry for each individual class. The particles from the best

class were re-extracted with a box size of 400 pixels and binned 2x and then subject to 3D

classification into 3 classes with a target resolution of 4Å. The particles from the top class were

combined and used for non-uniform refinement and local CTF refinement with the best volume

obtained from the 3D classification. The particle stack from the local CTF refinement was then

used for new round of non-uniform refinement, and then a new round of 3D classification was


<!-- Page 161 -->


147

performed with 3 classes at a target resolution of 3Å. The 3 classes were subject to a new round

of non-uniform refinement. Local CTF refinement was then performed the final particle stack and

then subjected to a new round of non-uniform refinement with C3 symmetry imposed. A new

round of local CTF refinement followed by non-uniform refinement in C3 symmetry was

performed and then subject to global CTF refinement follow by new round of non-uniform

refinement in C3 symmetry. The particles were re-extracted at full box size of 400 pixels without

binning and a new round of non-uniform refinement and local CTF refinement was performed.

This particle stack was used for a last non-uniform refinement with C3 symmetry and yielded a

reconstruction at 3Å nominal resolution. The two half-maps were used for sharpening in

DeepEMhancer45. The reported resolution is based on the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation

of 0.143 criterion.

Model building and refinement

The DeepEMhancer sharpened map was used for model building with ModelAngelo46 and then

manually built using COOT47. N-linked glycans were built manually in COOT using the glyco

extension and their stereochemistry and fit to the map validated with Privateer48. The model was

then refined in Phenix49 using real-space refinement and validated with MolProbity50.

## ABSTRACT

Exposure to pandemic influenza A viruses (IAVs) recalls memory B cells targeting conserved sites

on influenza hemagglutinin (HA). These memory B cells can undergo additional affinity

maturation through somatic hypermutation and affinity-dependent selection to increase pandemic

HA affinity. In the context of antigenically drifted HAs, affinity maturation of antibodies that target

the conserved receptor binding site (RBS) of HA increases affinity to the antigenically drifted

strain while maintaining or further increasing affinity to the “imprinting” HA that originally

elicited the antibody lineage. However, how affinity maturation of such an RBS-directed lineage

to a pandemic HA alters binding and neutralization breadth is unclear. In theory, further affinity

maturation could maintain or increase affinity to pre-pandemic strains, while gaining new affinity

to post-pandemic strains. Alternatively, affinity could remain biased towards the imprinting HA

while altering affinity to other strains. Here, we use in vitro affinity maturation of an RBS-directed

antibody, CH65, that was isolated prior to the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, to address how further affinity

maturation to a pandemic HA alters functional properties. We engineer Ramos B cells that can

somatically mutate antibody variable regions to display membrane bound CH65. We use these

cells to in vitro affinity mature CH65 to bind a post-pandemic HA, which required only one or two

amino acid mutations. The evolved CH65 variant displayed on the surface of B cells activates in

response to the post-pandemic HA and avid binding can be detected. However, monovalent binding

is weak and neutralization activity to a drifted pre-pandemic H1N1 IAV is lost. Notably, affinity

and neutralization potency remain high to the imprinting HA. We used deep mutational scanning

to demonstrate that the evolved CH65 variant retains a high barrier to escape in the context of the

imprinting IAV. These data suggest that this lineage is “specialized” for the imprinting HA but

minimal mutations are required to enable new, but weak, reactivity to a pandemic HA.

## INTRODUCTION

Zoonotic spillover of influenza A viruses (IAVs) from an animal reservoir have the

potential to cause pandemics when transmission is sustained. Broadly neutralizing antibodies

(bnAbs) that recognize conserved sites on influenza hemagglutinin (HA) serve as templates for

vaccine designs to elicit broadly protective antibody responses1. Characterization of HA-targeting

bnAbs has identified sites in the HA “head”2-9, which is responsible for sialic acid receptor binding,

and the “stem”10-16, which contains the fusion machinery. Although there are 18 HA subtypes, only

three (H1, H2 and H3) have caused IAV pandemics17, with the most recent pandemic as a result of

a swine H1N1 strain in 2009 that entered the human population, causing hundreds of thousands of

deaths18. Reassortment of IAV gene segments created the 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus with

hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) surface glycoproteins that have not circulated in the

human population, resulting in low pre-existing immunity. Although the post-pandemic HA is

significantly different than pre-pandemic HAs, exposure to the 2009 pandemic virus resulted in

recalling B cells that target conserved sites on the immunodominant HA head, namely the receptor

binding site (RBS) and lateral patch, that were elicited by prior exposure4,19,20.

Antibody responses to influenza draw from memory B cells that have previously

undergone the process of affinity maturation21-25, where cycles of mutation and subsequent and

selection within germinal centers ultimately increase the affinity for the targeted epitope26,27. The

enzyme activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) mutates cytosine to uracil, and the

subsequent DNA replication and repair machinery can introduce nucleotide substitutions that could

result in amino acid changes in the antibody variable regions that influence affinity28. This process

is not random, as AID targets certain regions more than others28. We have previously shown that

RBS-directed bnAbs gain breadth through affinity maturation to repeated IAV exposures, rather


<!-- Page 171 -->


157

than beginning with breadth29,30. Notably, affinity towards the IAV that originally elicited an

antibody lineage is typically the highest, which we refer to as the imprinting strain30,31. This is

consistent with the phenomenon of original antigenic sin32-35 or immune imprinting36, which

describes that serological recognition is biased towards a person’s first influenza exposure.

The prototypic RBS-directed bnAb, CH65, was isolated in 2008 prior to the 2009 H1N1

pandemic29,37,38. Unsurprisingly, CH65 does not neutralize post-pandemic H1 strains39. CH65 was

originally elicited by a strain similar to A/Massachusetts/1/1990 (MA90) and gained reactivity to

an antigenically drifted strain A/Solomon Islands/03/2006 (SI06), which was determined by

affinity measurements using the inferred UCA and affinity-matured counterparts40. Further affinity

maturation of CH65 to recognize a post-pandemic strain could, in theory, increase its breadth to

post-pandemic strains while maintaining affinity to pre-pandemic strains. However, the degree of

somatic mutation required for antibodies targeting conserved sites to overcome an antigenic shift

is unclear. Furthermore, how additional affinity maturation alters the binding and neutralization

properties to historical strains, including the imprinting strain, is not known.

Here, we use a B cell display system that expresses AID7.341, a version of AID with

increased catalytic activity, to further affinity mature CH65 in vitro to recognize a post-pandemic

HA. Introduction of a single amino acid mutation enabled avidity to the post-pandemic HA, which

was further increased upon a second mutation. Although binding of this variant could be detected

in avid formats, the variant weakly bound in monovalent formats. The evolved variant maintained

potent neutralization against the imprinted strain but had reduced affinity and no neutralization

activity to drifted pre-pandemic strain SI06. We additionally used a deep mutational scanning

library in the imprinting strain to test whether the barrier to escape changes upon additional affinity

maturation to a pandemic strain, which showed that the evolved variant maintains a high barrier


<!-- Page 172 -->


158

to escape in the imprinting strain. Minimal mutation of CH65 dramatically alters the affinity and

neutralization properties of a non-imprinting strain but retains high affinity to the imprinting strain.

Thus, further affinity maturation of this lineage demonstrates bias, or “commitment” to the

imprinting strain. These data additionally demonstrate that B cell recall to pandemic IAVs can

rapidly gain B cell activation with minimal mutations.

## RESULTS

Generation of a B cell-based directed evolution system

To generate a B cell-based directed evolution system, we first tested whether a previously

described Ramos cell line42 lost surface IgM as a surrogate of somatic mutation43. This Ramos B

cell line was engineered to express AID7.341, which has increased catalytic activity relative to

wild-type AID, under the control of doxycycline (named Ramos AID7.3in cells)42. We passaged

these cells in the presence or absence of doxycycline and compared the loss of IgM to wild-type

Ramos cells (Figure 4.1A). After six days of culturing, we observed the doxycycline-treated cells,

but not the untreated cells, lost cell surface IgM expression (~25%) (Figure 4.1A). In contrast,

wild-type Ramos cells, which have previously been used for in vitro affinity maturation, had a

negligible change in cell surface IgM expression in the same timeframe (Figure 4.1A). To

determine the feasibility of single cell sorting and cloning of these populations, we sorted single

cells and cultured them until they could be routinely maintained in cell culture. We extracted RNA

from these cells and sequenced the variable regions to determine the number of nucleotide

substitutions. Of three clones from the untreated population, all encoded wild-type variable

regions; of eight clones sequenced from the IgM+ doxycycline treated population, five encoded 1

or 2 nucleotide substitutions. (Figure 4.1B).

Affinity maturation of CH65 alters binding and neutralization properties

We next tested the monovalent binding kinetics of Fab fragments to MA90, SI06,

A/California/7/2009 (CA09), and MI15 HA heads by biolayer interferometry. Consistent with

activity. Although CH65 and CH65ND potently neutralized SN89 (an MA90-like strain), only

CH65 neutralized SI06, with CH65ND showing no neutralization activity against SI06 (Figure

4.4B).

## DISCUSSION

Here, we find that minimal affinity maturation of the RBS-directed bnAb CH65 enables

reactivity to a post-pandemic H1 on the surface of a B cell. A B cell line encoding expressing this

evolved variant, CH65ND, activates in response to HA antigens from 1990 to 2015. However, the

affinity to the strain used in selections, MI15, is weak, and addition of S55N and G56D mutations

into CH65 reduced affinity to SI06 such that neutralization activity is now absent. Despite weak

binding to SI06 and MI15, CH65ND maintains high affinity, neutralization potency, and escape

resistance to the strain that imprinted the lineage, MA90.

Previous studies have used Ramos B cells to affinity mature antibodies47, such as anti-HIV

bnAbs44,48, as well as non-immunoglobulin proteins49. Initial studies relied on endogenous AID

expression in wild-type Ramos cells to introduce mutations into the sequence of interest44,47,49.

However, Ramos cell lines are known to lose the ability to mutate over time due to decreasing

expression of AID50. To address this and increase the speed of generating an AID-mutagenized

library, we applied the same strategy to AID7.3in cells42. This resulted in rapid IgM loss, an indirect

measurement of somatic hypermutation. Notably, however, the mutations identified in CH65ND

only encoded G>A mutations, which is indicative of fixing uracil mutations by replication rather

than by DNA repair machinery that’s required for the full mutational spectrum of somatic

hypermutation28. Consistently, G>A mutations are the most likely variant in Ramos cells51 but

future efforts will need to address whether such engineered cell lines mimic other natural processes

of somatic hypermutation, such as base excision repair and mismatch repair28. Additionally, AID-

based mutagenesis of already mutated mAbs, such as CH65, may by somewhat limited as AID

hotspots may have already been mutated, limiting the mutability of the antibody variable genes52.


<!-- Page 184 -->


170

Studies of original antigenic sin32,33,53,54, or antigenic seniority55 identify that antibody titers

are typically highest to the strain that circulated near the donors’ childhoods, but titers to other

strains are more variable. If exposure to influenza largely draws from the memory B cell repertoire,

subsequent affinity maturation of cross-reactive antibodies could alter binding to historical strains.

Here, we show additional affinity maturation of a cross-reactive antibody lineage can alter

reactivity to other strains. However, the affinity to the likely imprinting strain of this lineage is

maintained. This demonstrates that despite broad reactivity, affinity maturation may bias, or

“commit”, to a certain evolutionary trajectories that reinforces the specificity encoded by the naive

antibody. Consistent with this idea, we previously found that natural affinity maturation of this

lineage occurred through hierarchical sets of mutations that increased the affinity to MA90 while

affording breadth to additional strains30. Altogether, we find that this RBS-directed antibody

lineage is “specialized” for the imprinting HA that originally elicited the lineage. Future studies

will be needed to investigate whether the minimal mutations that enable B cell activation in

response to the pandemic HA support further affinity maturation to the pandemic HA or whether

prior affinity maturation limits the ability to gain high affinity to a pandemic HA.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

Cell lines and media

Ramos RA1 (ATCC) and AID7.3in (a gift from David Schatz) were maintained in RPMI (ATCC

modification, ThermoFisher) supplemented with penicillin/streptomycin (ThermoFisher),

Normocin (Invivogen), and 10-20% tetracycline-free “Tet-system approved” FBS (ThermoFisher)

to prevent unintended activation of doxycycline. When inducing expression of AID7.3,

doxycycline hyclate (Sigma) was added at a concentration of 200 ng/ml. All Ramos cells were

split every 2-3 days and maintained a cell density less than 2 x 106 cells per ml.

Protein production

HA or antibody variable regions were cloned with C-terminal tags. HA trimers contained C-

terminal tags 3C cleavage site/His tag/foldon/AviTag. Monomeric HA heads contained C-terminal

tags 3C cleavage site/His tag/AviTag. Full-length antibody and Fab fragment heavy chains

Between rounds, Ramos AID7.3in cells with CH66 knocked-in were passaged twice,

Biolayer interferometry

Fab affinities were determined by loading Fabs onto Fab2G sensors on an Octet RED96e

(Sartorius). All solutions had a final concentration of 0.1% BSA and 0.01% Tween20 in PBS. The

plates were equilibrated for 20 minutes in the instrument at 30 °C prior to acquiring data. Data was

acquired using the following protocol: 60s baseline; 60s Fab loading; 60s baseline; 6m association,

6m dissociation. Each interaction was tested with a six-fold titration series with 5 µM HA head as

the highest concentration. The data were fit to a 1:1 binding model in the Sartorius software to

determine kinetic parameters.

Antibodies were coated on 96-well high binding plates (Corning) at 5 µg/ml overnight at

RNA was isolated from Ramos cells using the AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini kit (Qiagen). The

Deep mutational scanning escape assays were performed as described in Chapter 2. Briefly,

A/Siena/10/1989 deep mutational scanning virus libraries were complexed with 10x the IC99

## Summary

Viral escape from antibody-mediated immunity enables viruses to continually evolve within the

human population. Repeated infections and vaccinations over an individual’s lifetime recall B cell

responses elicited by prior exposures, especially a person’s first exposure, attempting to re-use past

antibodies or update them through affinity maturation to make them more effective. The utility of

these imprinted antibodies has been debated over the past seven decades with some proposing

strategies to harness the effect1 and others devising ways to avoid it2. This is partly because

antibodies with “original antigenic sin” phenotypes can have both beneficial and detrimental

effects. For example, antibodies usually have lower affinity to strains from secondary exposures

compared to the strains that originally elicited them3,4 and can bind conserved, but poorly

protective epitopes. However, imprinted monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) can also bind functionally

conserved, neutralizing, and protective epitopes5-12. Studies have demonstrated that broadly

neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), which guide vaccine design, originally recognize a limited

number of strains but gain breadth through affinity maturation5,6,8,13-16, consistent with an

imprinting phenotype. Next-generation vaccine designs aim to elicit these bnAbs that target

conserved epitopes. However, there is limited knowledge about how viruses escape imprinted

bnAbs targeting conserved sites. In this thesis, we assessed viral escape in the context of imprinted

antibody responses and bnAbs binding conserved sites.

In Chapter 2, we addressed how affinity maturation and recall of imprinted antibodies influences

the ability of the influenza virus to escape. We selected imprinted mAb lineages that target the

conserved receptor binding site (RBS) or lateral patch of influenza hemagglutinin (HA) and

determined viral escape from the imprinting and drifted strains. We did this by generating deep


<!-- Page 197 -->


183

mutational scanning (DMS) viral libraries of the HA head, which includes all single amino acid

mutations and deletions, and passaged these viruses in the presence of the unmutated common

ancestor (UCA) or affinity-matured mAbs to determine the enrichment of each amino acid variant.

We found that affinity maturation of these lineages raised the barrier to escape. However,

antigenically drifted strains had a low barrier to escape from these mAbs even though they had

similar neutralization activity. Structural characterization of affinity maturation and escape showed

antibody “tilting” is one mechanism by which a mAb can raise the barrier to escape; the loss of

antibody-antigen contacts during viral evolution can likewise lower the barrier to escape. These

data have several important conclusions for next-generation vaccine and therapeutic designs. First,

affinity maturation of mAbs targeting the RBS has the potential to increase the barrier to escape.

This suggests one strategy is to predict new variants through experimental and/or computational

methods. Immunization strategies that incorporate predicted variants may allow affinity

maturation to compensate for viral escape mutations and “cut off” those escape pathways. Second,

our data supports the notion that imprinted mAbs are both beneficial and detrimental. Although

there were more viral escape mutations for imprinted mAbs in the drifted strain, some maintained

potent neutralization activity, suggesting these mAbs contribute to protection. However, in general

mAbs had weaker neutralization against the contemporary strain. This suggests that the overall

antibody response may have non-optimal neutralization activity. Future vaccine designs will need

to take this balance into consideration. Third, because the imprinting strain has the highest barrier

to escape, immunogen design strategies that “guide” the affinity maturation process may ultimately

increase the barrier to escape to the original immunizing antigen, which is sometimes a non-natural

or engineered protein, but not the terminal boosting antigen17. These strategies may ultimately

generate bnAbs for which naturally occurring viral strains have a low barrier to escape.


<!-- Page 198 -->


184

In Chapter 3, we isolated human pan-subtype neutralizing mAbs to the H1 head, H3 head, and

group 2 stem. The pan-H1 mAbs derive from a class of mAbs that target the lateral patch10,18.

Consistent with previous reports, these mAbs use the antibody variable genes VH3-23/VK1-33 but

carry distinct somatic mutations and CDRH3 sequences. Because experimental, next-generation

vaccines have been shown to elicit mAbs targeting this site in animal models19, these strategies

will likely elicit this class of mAbs if used in humans. We therefore mapped recognition of these

mAbs by viral escape, which identified positions and specific mutations that escape this class of

mAb. Although these mAbs target conserved sites and currently provide pan-H1N1 neutralization

activity, redirection of the antibody response to this site will likely drive escape. Because there is

limited immune pressure at this site currently, we affinity-matured one of these mAbs in vitro for

potential clinical use, which increased the neutralization potency. We additionally identified a pan-

subtype mAb targeting the H3 head. This mAb, ADI-85647, targets a similar site as the lateral

patch on the side of the HA head, which overlaps with the site targeted by another mAb, H3v-4720.

Although these mAbs have different reactivity profiles, variable gene usages, and modes of

recognition, both mAbs engage a conserved pocket shown to have low mutational tolerance21. The

group 2 stem-targeting mAb binds an epitope at the base of the HA stem and overlaps with other

group 2 mAbs22,23, but extends its CDRH3 to create distinct contacts. The results from this chapter

also have implications for next-generation vaccine design. First, conservation does not necessarily

equate to a high barrier to escape. For example, the pan-H1 mAbs target a site that is conserved

across ~100 years of H1N1 strains, but that has no defined function. Escape from these H1 mAbs

were largely consistent between strains, identifying positions that can readily escape these mAbs.

Thus, vaccine design needs to consider the implications for viral escape, not simply generating

antibodies targeting conserved sites. Second, the pan-H3 mAbs target conserved sites that overlap


<!-- Page 199 -->


185

with previously characterized mAbs but are unique. These data highlight the benefit of a polyclonal

antibody response targeting these sites, as they may have distinct escape profiles. Together, vaccine

and therapeutic designs need to consider how an elicited antibody response may drive viral escape.

In my opinion, broad antibody responses generated by current vaccine designs are likely to be

readily escaped and may not provide the desired goal of long-lasting and broad protection because

viral evolution at these targeted sites is a consequence of minimal immune pressure, rather than

the inability to evolve.

In Chapter 4, we begin to explore the effects of affinity maturation of the mAb CH65 that targets

the RBS of HA. We used a Ramos B cell system that expresses an activation-induced cytidine

deaminase variant with increased catalytic activity24,25 to mutagenize the variable regions of CH65

knocked-in to the endogenous immunoglobulin loci. This B cell line activates in response to

historical strains, but very weakly towards a post-2009 pandemic influenza strain (MI15),

consistent with the isolation of CH65 in 2008. From the AID-mutagenized library, we selected

CH65 variants that gained affinity to MI15 through one to two amino acid substitutions. A cell line

bearing the evolved CH65ND variant activates similarly in response to either historical strains or

MI15. However, monovalent affinity of CH65ND  is ~1000-fold weaker compared to the imprinting

strain, MA90, and loses ~10-fold affinity to an antigenically drifted strain, SI06. CH65ND

maintained potent neutralization to MA90, but lost activity to SI06. Furthermore, the barrier to

escape from CH65ND is high, similar to CH65, as shown in Chapter 2. These data highlight that

affinity maturation of an imprinted antibody lineage can alter neutralization potency and breadth

but remains “committed”, or “specialized”, to the original eliciting strain.


<!-- Page 200 -->
